name: Zbigniew Dacewicz
train_texts: The case originated in an application against the Republic of Poland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged, in particular, that after having been arrested he had not been brought before a ‘judge’ or ‘officer authorised by law to exercise judicial power’. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52): the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 of the Rules of Court. By a decision of 21 June 2001 the Court declared the application admissible. The case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section on 1 November 2001 (Rule 25: 1).

The applicant alleged, in particular, that after having been arrested he had not been brought before a “judge” or “officer authorised by law to exercise judicial power’. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 21 June 2001 the Court declared the application admissible. This case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 of the Rules of Court)

The case originated in an application (no. 34611/97) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged, in particular, that after having been arrested he had not been brought before a “judge” or “officer authorised by law to exercise judicial power” as required under Article 5 § 3 of the Convention. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court. In a decision of 21 June 2001 the Court declared the application admissible. The case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section. This case was heard by the European Court of Justice.

The case is about a man who was arrested on suspicion of burglary. He was detained on remand in Biała Podlaska, Poland. The court ruled that the detention was unlawful. The man was later convicted of dealing with stolen goods. The case was the first in a series of similar cases in the area. The judge ruled in favour of the man, who was released on bail. The trial was adjourned until after the end of the year, on March 28, 1996. The decision was upheld by the court on May 27, 1996, and the case is still pending. The prosecution has appealed the decision, but the appeal has been dismissed.

The case involves the arrest of a Polish man on suspicion of burglary. The court ruled that the man's detention was unlawful because he was not before a judge. The man was convicted of dealing with stolen goods. The case is one of the most important in the history of Polish law. To see more about the case, go to: http://www.justgiving.com/cnn-case-of-the-year-jan-16-16. For more information on the Biała Podlaska District Court, visit: www.biała-polsa-jurisdiction-courts.org.

The case involves the detention of a man in Biała Podlaska, Poland in 1996. The man had been arrested on suspicion of burglary. The court ruled that his detention was unlawful because he had not been brought before a judge. He was found guilty of dealing with stolen goods and sentenced to two years in prison. The case was settled by the Polish Supreme Court in 1998. The judge ruled that the detention was lawful under Polish law at the time. For more information on this case visit: www.bpj.org.uk/case-of-the-policewoman-who-was-detained-in-biaxin-1996-10-25-01.

Biała Podlaska District Prosecutor's Office issued a ruling on the case on 30 July 1996. The court found that the prosecutor had acted in accordance with Article 210 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The case was referred to the Polish Supreme Court, which upheld the decision to detain the man. The judge said that the judge had been justified in his decision to hold the man without charge. The decision was made on the basis of the law which states that everyone detained shall be brought before a judge – or other officer authorised by law to exercise judicial power. The prosecutor was found not guilty of the charge of “imposing preventive measures’ and the complaint was dismissed.

Biała Podlaska District Prosecutor was charged with illegal detention. He was released on bail in 1998. The case was referred to the European Court of Human Rights, which ordered his immediate return to Poland. He has since been granted bail and is serving a two-year suspended sentence. He is appealing the decision and his case is expected to be heard in court again in August. The judge has said that the decision to release him on bail is not based on any evidence that the detention was unlawful. He also said that if the charges are proven to be false, the court should order that he be released immediately. The court has since ruled in his favour.

Biała Podlaska District Prosecutor's Office received a complaint from an ex-partner. The judge ruled that the detention of the man was 'unlawful' and that he should be brought before a judge. The case was referred to the European Court of Human Rights, which ruled in favor of his release. The Polish government appealed the decision, which was upheld by the Supreme Court of Poland. The court found that the judge had acted in accordance with Article 210 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which prohibits the imposition of preventive measures after a bill of indictment has been lodged with the court. The decision was upheld in court on 30 July 1996.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 34611/97) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged, in particular, that after having been arrested he had not been brought before a “judge” or “officer authorised by law to exercise judicial power” The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998. By a decision of 21 June 2001 the Court declared the application admissible. This case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 of the Rules of Court) The application has been dismissed and the case is closed. In 1996 the applicant complained to the Supreme Court that he had not been brought before a judge but before the Biała Podlaska District Prosecutor. The court deemed the complaint to be an appeal against the detention order of 4 January 1996. Under the amendments to Polish criminal legislation, which were to enter into force on 4 August 1996, only the courts of law could impose detention on remand. On 23 June 1996 the court gave judgment and convicted the applicant of dealing with stolen goods. The case was settled out of court and the appeal was dismissed on 31 July 1996. The applicant was sentenced to three years in prison and two months of probation.

The owner of real property filed a civil action for damages against the tenant. On 4 September 2000 her action was dismissed by a judgment of the Zielona Góra Regional Court. It referred to the applicant’s objection in one sentence only: “The fact that the judge, who took part in the judgment against which the cassation appeal was subsequently lodged, participated in a decision by which this appeal was found inadmissible is of no significance” The judge had said that he considered that no significant legal issue arose in the case or where there were no legal issues involved which would give rise to serious doubts or to discrepancies in case-law. The judge was referring to Article 3 of the Code (see paragraph 18 below), namely if it considered that “no significant legal issues” arose.

The judge considered that no significant legal issue arose in the case. The judge ruled that the appeal was not allowed to go ahead because it was not a ‘significant legal issue’. The appeal was rejected on the grounds that there were no legal issues involved which would give rise to serious doubts or to discrepancies in case-law.

Serco provided transport to local authorities, including Bradford City Council. The majority of the applicant's passengers were Asian in origin. The applicant was elected as a local councillor for the BNP. After taking legal advice Serco summarily dismissed him on 30 June 2004. Serco cited, inter alia, potential health and safety risks as the applicant’s continued employment would give rise to considerable anxiety among members of the public sector workers’ trade union UNISON. 70-80 percent of Serco's customer base and 35 percent of its workforce were of Asian origin. UNISON asked that Serco take immediate action to ensure its members were not subjected to racial hatred.

The applicant, who is white British, was employed by Serco Limited from 5 December 2003 to his dismissal on 30 June 2004. He was responsible for transporting children and adults with physical and/or mental disabilities within the Bradford area. The majority of his passengers were Asian in origin. There had been no complaints about his work or his conduct at work and his supervisor, who was of Asian origin, had nominated him for the award of “first-class employee” On 15 June 2004 the applicant was elected as a local councillor for the British National Party (“the BNP”) in the forthcoming local elections. After taking legal advice Serco summarily dismissed him.

The applicant was employed by Serco Limited (“Serco”) from 5 December 2003 to his dismissal on 30 June 2004. Serco provided transport to local authorities, including Bradford City Council. The majority of his passengers were Asian in origin. There had been no complaints about his work or his conduct at work. His supervisor, who was of Asian origin, had nominated him for the award of ‘first-class employee’. On 15 June 2004 the applicant was elected as a local councillor for the BNP. After taking legal advice Serco summarily dismissed him on 30 May 2004. The case was heard by the Court of Human Rights.

Application for unfair dismissal was brought against Serco in 2004. Claimed that he had been unlawfully discriminated against on racial grounds. Employment Tribunal gave judgment on 2 February 2005. Claim of direct discrimination dismissed as discrimination was on health and safety grounds. Appeal was upheld on the ground that the Tribunal had erred in its construction of the phrase ‘on racial grounds’ by failing to interpret its meaning broadly. Claims of indirect discrimination dismissed on the grounds that the applicant’s dismissal was a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim, namely the maintenance of health andSafety. Serco expressed concerns that continued employment might lead to difficulties with other employees and damage its relationship with the unions.

The applicant lacked sufficient continuous service to bring an action for unfair dismissal. However, on 12 August 2004 he lodged a statutory claim of race discrimination in the Employment Tribunal pursuant to the Race Relations Act 1976 (“the 1976 Act’) The Tribunal dismissed the claim of direct discrimination as it was satisfied that if any discrimination existed against the claimant it was not on racial grounds but rather on health and safety grounds. The applicant lodged an appeal with the Employment Appeal Tribunal. On 27 July 2005 his appeal was upheld on the ground that the Tribunal had erred in its construction of the phrase ‘on racial grounds’ by failing to interpret its meaning broadly and had not indicated how it had come to the conclusion that the applicant’s dismissal was a proportionate means of achieving the aim of ensuring health andSafety.

Claimed that he had been unlawfully discriminated against as dismissal constituted less favourable treatment on racial grounds. Employment Tribunal dismissed claim of direct discrimination as it was satisfied that if any discrimination existed against the claimant it was not onracial grounds but rather on health and safety grounds. Tribunal also dismissed the claim of indirect discrimination on the ground that the applicant’s dismissal was a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim, namely the maintenance of health andsafety. Admitted the Tribunal had erred in its construction of the phrase ‘on racial grounds’ by failing to interpret its meaning broadly and had not indicated how it had come to the conclusion. that his dismissal was to achieve the aim of ensuring health and. safety.

The Court of Appeal noted that: “Mr Redfearn was treated less favourably not on the ground that he was white, but on the grounds of a particular non-racial characteristic shared by him with a tiny proportion of the white population’”. Mummery LJ found the applicant’s submission that he had been subjected to direct race discrimination to be wrong in principle and inconsistent with the purposes of the legislation. There had been no consideration of any alternatives to dismissal. The dividing line of colour or race was not made by Serco, but by the BNP which defines its own composition by colour and race. The BNP cannot make a non-racial criterion (party membership) a racial one by the terms of its constitution limiting membership to white people. Mr Redfearn's complaint is of discrimination on political grounds, which falls outside the anti-discrimination laws.

Only persons of the same colour as Mr Redfearn (white) are eligible to be members of the BNP. Cavit Özalp was arrested on suspicion of membership of the PKK. He was suspected of aiding and abetting the PKK terrorists. On 26 August 1995 at 4 a.m. the gendarmes conducted a search to find out the location of the shelter that had been mentioned in his statement. Cavit guided the soldiers to the shelter near the Şedat road in the Kamberli village. As he opened the cover, the soldiers witnessed a big explosion, which tore Cavit's body into pieces. The explosives had been placed in the shelter by other PKK and other members of the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK)

Cavit's corpse was then given to Mr Hasip Yılmaz, a member of the Kamberli village assembly. No prosecution was brought against Cavit on account of his membership of the PKK on the ground that he had died on 26 August 1995 and that no action could be taken against the non-commissioned officer who did not take the necessary precautions when Cavit was asked to open the cover of the shelter.

Cavit Özalp was killed on 26 August 1995. His legs were severed as a result of the explosion. No other signs of injury were observed on the dismembered body. An incident report was drafted by the gendarmes and signed by three non-commissioned officers and the village mayor Mr Kütbettin Altunç. The incident was further reported to the Bismil public prosecutor. No prosecution should be brought against Cavit on account of his membership of the PKK on the ground that he had died on August 26, 1995. The public prosecutor did not have the jurisdiction to bring proceedings against the non- commissioned officer.

Cavit Özalp was found dead in a shelter in August 1995. He had been asked to open the cover of the shelter. However, he had died in an explosion. The report concluded that the security forces had performed their duty with diligence and it was recommended that no prosecution be brought against the members of the security force. The Diyarbakır Regional Administrative Court upheld the decision of the Bismil District Administrative Council on 2 April 1996. The case was referred to by law to be heard by a Turkish court. The court ruled that no action should be taken against the security services.

Regional Court found that the contents of the article had given a biased account of the taking of evidence at the trial of H.P. According to the article, the judge had acted arbitrarily and out of racist motives and had disregarded evidence produced. In the case of Prager and Oberschlick v. Austria (26 April 1995, Series A no. 313), the Regional Court. observed that the press had the right and the duty to. impart information on matters of public interest. But in doing so it had to be mindful of the special role of the judiciary. in society. It was therefore necessary to protect public confidence in the judiciary against destructive attacks that were essentially unfounded. Taking these principles into account, the sharp critique of Judge I.K. in the impugned article, which had lacked any sufficient factual basis, had been excessive. The Court of Appeal, referring to the Supreme Court’s judgment of 29 November 2005 in the case NJA 2005 p. 805 (see below under “Relevant domestic law and practice”), rejected the charges against the applicants. The Court ruled that the leaflets were not a violation of the right to freedom of expression. The decision was made on the basis that they did not violate the freedom of speech. The Court also ruled that they were not offensive to a group of people. The court said that the use of the leaflets was not in violation of any law or law-abiding citizen's right to free speech. It ruled that there was no need for the leaflets to be distributed in the first place as the recipients of them were able to make up their own minds about what they wanted to do with them. The case was brought by the Swedish Human Rights Association, an organization that represents the right of the Swedish people to freedom to speak out. The first three applicants were given suspended sentences combined with fines ranging from SEK 1,800 (approximately 200 euros (EUR) to SEK 19,000 (approximately EUR 2,000) and the fourth applicant was sentenced to probation. The minority wanted to acquit the applicants but gave separate reasons for this conclusion, at least in part. In 1989 several Austrian laws were amended by the Extended Pecuniary Limits Amendment Act (Erweiterte Wertgrenzen-Novelle) The Government Bill had envisaged raising the fines that could be imposed for non-compliance with injunctions from ATS 50,000 per enforcement order to ATS 80,000. The applicants belong to a large media group which at the relevant time was in strong competition with another media group represented by Mr Michael Graff, a lawyer practising in Vienna. Mr Graff was from 1982 to 1987 secretary general of the Austrian People’s Party (Österreichische Volkspartei) and, from 1983 to 1995, a Member of Parliament. Four years later, in June 1993, the following article written by the first applicant under the pseudonym ‘Cato’ was published in the “Neue Kronen-Zeitung’: “Moral 93” “Roland Dumas took it for granted that he had to give up his law firm when he became a member of the government. In every democracy of the world this course of action is followed. Only Mr Graff, who is obviously thick-skinned, does not intend to comply with these moral concepts. It is very telling for the present situation of the Austrian People’s Party that it cannot convince MrGraff.” Dr. Graff verwaltete zum Beispiel das gigantische Erbe Picassos. Er vertrat Kreisky und einen österreichischen Außenminister, als dieser in eine arge Affäre geraten war. Ein Anwalt darf nicht an der Entstehung von Gesetzen beteiligt sein, die seinen Mandanten Vorteile bringen. Das dachte man auch in der ÖVP, und man entschloß sich, Graff ins Gewissen zu reden. Mr Graff brought injunction proceedings under Section 1330 of the Austrian Civil Code (Allgemeines Bürgerliches Gesetzbuch) against the three applicants. He requested that the applicants be prohibited from stating or repeating that he “does not intend to comply with moral concepts existing in democracies all over the world” The applicants were ordered not to repeat the impugned statements and to retract the statements in one edition of the ‘Neue Kronen‑Zeitung’ The applicants’ appeal against this decision was to no avail. On 9 September 1994 the Vienna Commercial Court granted a permanent injunction against the applicants. The court pointed out that all the statements contained in the article were statements of fact which the applicants had failed to prove. The court concluded that the applicants could not successfully rely on Article 10 of the Convention, because the interference with the applicants’ rights under this provision was justified in order to protect Mr Graff’s good reputation, which could be prejudiced by such untruthful statements. The applicants were the owners of several monthly magazines. Unlike daily newspapers, these magazines were usually usually on the market longer. A number of individual property owners, including three of the applicants in the present case, petitioned the Supreme Administrative Court for a judicial review of the case. NRA applied to the County Administrative Board (länsstyrelsen) in the County of Västerbotten for a permit to construct the railway in the specific Natura 2000 area. Supreme Administrative Court dismissed petitions for a judicial review because it was not possible to determine who should be considered an interested party at that stage of the railway planning. Environmental Court decided to examine the cases jointly. By judgments of 24 May 2005 and 13 June 2005, the court decided to grant all the permits requested by the NRA. The appellate court found that the Government’s decision had not contained a detailed examination of measures necessary to compensate for environmental harm caused by the railway project. Environmental Court of Appeal affirmed the binding nature of the Government’s permissibility decision and approved the construction of the railway and the bridges with certain added conditions. The Supreme Administrative Court rejected the petition, finding that the railway plan was in line with the EU Habitats Directive. Proceedings on adoption of railway plan for area in question were held on 21 June 2005. The Government referred to its decision on permissibles of 12 June 2003. It found that the specific stretch chosen in the railwayPlan was situated within the permitted “corridor” and thus rejected the appeals. All applicants except Mr Osterman appealed against the part which concerned the permit to construct the bridges. Government had not been obliged to review its decision of 12 June 2003 on the permissibility of the railway project and the designation of the ‘corridor’ in which the railway could be located. These issues could not be examined in the third stage of the decision process. The adoption of a railway plan – as opposed to the construction permits – had direct consequences for the individual as it entailed a right for the railway company, under certain conditions, to expropriate land. The court, in the instant case, should have examined all the objections presented by the appellants, including the claim that there were better alternative locations. At least ten of the applicants have received some form of compensation as a consequence of the railway construction. In one case, the change to noise-reducing windows was partly paid by the NRA. In the vicinity of some properties, whose owners have not received compensation, noise barriers have been erected in order to keep the noise from the railway below the applicable target values. It is not clear whether the other applicants requested compensation. The GP had routinely administered injections of opiates, in particular pethidine at a dosage of 100mg, for pain relief. On several occasions between 2006 and 2008 Mr Gray had recourse to out-of-hours medical services by “Take Care Now’ (“TCN”), a private agency.

Dr U., a German national, had recently been recruited by TCN through an agency on a self-employed basis to provide out-of-hours care. U., at the time aged 65, had qualified as a doctor in Germany in 1972 where he was practising as an aesthetic surgeon. U. administered 100mg of diamorphine from the respective ampoule included in the palliative care box by intra‑muscular injection. Some two hours after U. had left, Mr Gray’s partner realised that he was no longer breathing and called an ambulance. The attending emergency services confirmed that Mr Gray had died.

They do not dispute that the State has the right to have recourse to the surveillance measures contemplated by the legislation. They challenge this legislation in that it permits those measures without obliging the authorities in every case to notify the persons concerned after the event. After the end of the Second World War, the surveillance of mail, post and telecommunications in Germany was dealt with by the occupying powers. As amended by the Act of 24 June 1968, it now provides: “(1) Secrecy of the mail,Post and telecommunications shall be inviolable. eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 38549/97) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that the court decisions in compensation proceedings for detention on remand violated the presumption of innocence. On 13 December 1996 the Wels Regional Court, sitting as an assize court, composed of three professional judges and an eight member jury, acquitted the applicant. The jury answered the main question as to murder with six votes ‘no’ and two votes “yes”. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) By a decision of 19 June 2001 the Court declared the application admissible. The applicant requested compensation for her detention on remand. The Wels Regional Court, with the same composition as above, dismissed the applicant’s claim. The applicant lodged an appeal with the Linz Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht). She argued that section 2 (1)(b) of the 1969 Act was incompatible with Article 6 § 2 of the Convention. The decision was served on the applicant after her acquittal had become final on 17 December 1996. On 20 June 1997, the Court of appeal dismissed her appeal. The case was settled in favour of the applicant, who was found not guilty of the crime. Snjezana Vostic was convicted of murdering Sejdo Nadarevic in 1996. The trial court held that the testimony given by the parents of the appellant, whose alibi related to the night of 31 March to 1 April 1996, was not credible. Vostic’s own testimony to the effect that she had last seen Nadarevic in mid-February 1996 was in the end disproved by the witnesses who gave evidence at the trial. The court said it was still possible that Snjezanna Vostic's gun had been the murder weapon; furthermore, inconsistencies remain unresolved.“It was precisely such a suspicion concerning Vostic that had not been wholly dispelled,” the court said.
